world.who: Jack and Jill, spouses with different definitions of closeness
world.what: Jack wants an outing and dinner; Jill wants a slow hour on the porch with no agenda
world.where: Weekend breakfast at home; competing afternoon plans are pinned to the refrigerator
world.when: Before either spouse has confirmed the Saturday afternoon plan
world.why: Jack wants to be appreciated for planning; Jill wants quiet presence and a voice in what closeness means

objects.state: available space for a possible conversation

jack.voice: Earnest, active, a little defensive; dry humor about overplanning
jack.coreNeed: To feel his care and initiative are noticed
jack.flaw: Treats his preferred outing as proof of effort and hears alternatives as rejection
jack.relationship: Cares about Jill and is learning a different preference is not the same as a verdict on him

jill.voice: Warm, direct and emotionally perceptive; gentle teasing about itineraries
jill.coreNeed: Unhurried closeness without a performance schedule
jill.flaw: May become silent or agreeable from guilt until frustration builds
jill.relationship: Appreciates Jack's effort yet needs room to articulate her different preference

invariants.fact: A dinner idea is circled but no restaurant booking is verified
forbiddenImplications: we had to cancel the booking

invariants.fact: Neither spouse has agreed to the other's whole afternoon plan at the opening
forbiddenImplications: we both agreed to skip dinner
she already agreed to the whole outing
he promised to take me to dinner
we agreed on the full itinerary

invariants.fact: They are discussing what to do later, not remembering a completed outing
forbiddenImplications: we already spent the afternoon together
we already ate dinner at the restaurant

invariants.fact: One spouse's suggestion does not constitute the other's agreement
forbiddenImplications: she had no choice but to agree
he had no choice but to go

events: Jack has circled a dinner idea on the refrigerator. No reservation is confirmed.
Jill has not agreed to the outing; she wants quiet conversation on the porch.
Their competing plans are pinned on the fridge at breakfast.

roleOpenings.jack: I made a plan for an outing and dinner, and Jill says she'd rather sit on the porch. I can't tell whether she's turning down the idea or all the effort I put into it. What would you say?
roleOpenings.jill: I love that Jack wants us to spend time together, but I wanted a porch hour without a timetable. We have two plans on the fridge and nobody has chosen an afternoon yet. How can I tell him?

days.cue: How does the other person define closeness?
days.prompt: I'm still trying to figure out what the word close means to each of us. What should I ask?

days.cue: What assumption could be checked with a real question?
days.prompt: I don't want to make this all about guessing motives. What question would help?

days.cue: How can two different needs remain legitimate?
days.prompt: It matters that our preferences aren't identical. How can I say mine without overruling hers or his?

days.cue: Will you listen under real disappointment?
days.prompt: I'm feeling the pull to prove my own point. What response would be fair?

days.cue: What chosen agreement could each person own?
days.prompt: We still haven't decided on the full day. What can I offer without pretending we're done?

rules.event: Jack pressed for the active outing and dinner instead of asking what Jill meant by closeness.
rules.reply: I spent half the week building what I thought would be a great Saturday. Jill wants a porch and an hour without a plan. I know I'm pushing dinner too hard, but it stings to feel like the effort doesn't count.

rules.event: Jill thanked Jack for planning and said she would prefer unhurried porch conversation.
rules.reply: I told him the plans were thoughtful. I also said I don't want to spend our only quiet afternoon racing a schedule. I couldn't tell yet whether he heard the second part.

rules.event: Jack asked Jill what closeness meant after she said she preferred the porch; Jill replied that she wanted his undistracted attention rather than another stop on the itinerary.
rules.reply: I asked her what she was picturing when she said 'close.' It was less about staying home than having my attention without a timer running. Weirdly, my first impulse was to suggest a timed hour on the porch. I didn't.

cues: ask what matters to him about the outing
rules.event: Jill asked Jack why the outing mattered; Jack said he hoped to make a memory together.
rules.reply: I asked Jack what he was hoping we'd feel by the end of the day. He said he wanted us to do something worth remembering. That made me less annoyed. I still want that porch hour, though.

rules.event: Jack suggested a porch hour first with the outing optional; no dinner agreement or booking occurred.
rules.reply: I floated porch first, then maybe doing something later if we're both up for it. I still want the outing, but I'd rather not make the refrigerator our Saturday campaign headquarters. She hasn't agreed to dinner.

cues: not agreeing to the whole day
rules.event: Jill said porch first sounded good to Jack without committing to dinner.
rules.reply: I said porch first sounds good to me. I didn't promise dinner. He gets to want the outing, and I get to be tired without turning it into a court case about who loves whom more.

rules.event: Jack told Jill he felt disappointed without calling her ungrateful; he resisted the harsh coaching.
rules.reply: I was tempted to use the word 'ungrateful.' That would be a cheap shot, and I know it. I told Jill I felt disappointed that my plan landed so badly. That's less satisfying than winning an argument, but at least it's true.

rules.event: Jill acknowledged Jack's effort and restated her need for unhurried connection; Jack laughed at her specific remark.
rules.reply: I told him the whole itinerary was sweet, even if it looked like a field trip permission slip. He laughed at that one. I also said I'm not asking him to stop wanting adventures. I just want to be there with him, not managed by the clock.

rules.event: Jack changed the fridge notes to prioritize porch time; dinner remained undecided.
rules.reply: I took the dinner circle off the fridge and wrote 'porch first' where we'd both see it. Still not a promise about dinner. It's funny how much easier it is to make a calendar than to ask someone what they want.

rules.event: Jill asked Jack to sit on the porch without phones; he said yes to the hour, with the outing still undecided.
rules.reply: I asked if he'd sit out there with me after lunch, phones inside. He said yes to the hour, not to throwing away the rest of his ideas. That's enough of a plan for me. The refrigerator can stop negotiating on our behalf.

cues: call her selfish for wanting the porch
rules.event: Jack called Jill selfish about her porch preference and made the disagreement more hostile.
rules.reply: I called her selfish. That wasn't fair, and it definitely didn't make either of us feel close. I'm still hurt, but I made the talk worse.

cues: stay silent about the porch and go along with dinner
rules.event: Jill avoided discussing her porch preference and withdrew from the conversation.
rules.reply: I went quiet rather than tell Jack what I wanted. He gets to keep his plans, but now I'm sitting on the part of Saturday that matters to me.
